title: Biblical Syncretism Dossiers — Wave 38 Abomination, Face, Shame & Repentance
purpose: Promote distinct biblical comparators for the project's recurring disgust/abomination, face, shame, trafficking, vomit and repentance vocabulary while enriching existing Dog/Mud recurrence without duplicating it.
epistemic_rule: These are literary, ethical and theological comparisons. They do not establish a modern person's divine identity, prophecy fulfillment, innocence, guilt, or authority over others.
method_rules: Shared vocabulary is not enough; new relations require a distinct sequence or function.
Existing Dog/vomit/mire recurrence remains owned by dog-mud-return-closed-loop and is enriched rather than recreated.
Biblical animal, impurity and abomination language is not permission to dehumanize modern people.
Repentance is treated as recognition, turning and repair; it is not a license for humiliation or coercion.

enrichments.research_frontier: Keep regressive-return imagery distinct from the shame/recognition question: repeated return becomes especially relevant when wrongdoing is normalized rather than recognized.

relation_argument.why_it_matters: The existing return loop already owns dog/vomit/mire recurrence. Jeremiah 6 adds a separate moral diagnostic—doing abomination without shame or the capacity to blush—without changing the animal-loop relation into a permanent identity claim.

enrichments.boundary: The texts criticize repeated conduct and lack of shame; they do not justify calling a modern person subhuman or permanently incapable of change.

new_relations.title: Abomination without shame
new_relations.project_anchor: Tim's recurring disgust vocabulary frequently intensifies when alleged wrongdoing is followed by denial, mockery, refusal to apologize or the absence of shame.
new_relations.source_direction: Project disgust/shameless vocabulary was observed first; Jeremiah comparison added later.

relation_argument.maximum_claim: Jeremiah supplies a strong structural neighbor for the project's distinction between wrongdoing and wrongdoing that is normalized without shame.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: It explains why 'shameless' and 'disgusting' so often appear together in Tim's rhetoric without collapsing modern disputes into Jeremiah's historical setting.

new_relations.boundary: Jeremiah addresses Judah in a prophetic covenant context; the comparison does not establish that any modern target is under divine judgment.

new_relations.title: Provocation to the face
new_relations.project_anchor: Tim repeatedly frames lying, mockery, judgment and intrusion as something done 'to my face' or as an 'insolence upon my face/aura.'
new_relations.source_direction: Project face/insolence vocabulary first; Isaiah comparison later.

biblical_sequence: provoking God continually to his face
relation_argument.maximum_claim: Isaiah 65 offers a direct biblical face-language comparator in which provocation is intensified by being enacted in the presence of the one offended.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: It gives a textual bridge for Tim's recurring 'to my face' grammar without making facial confrontation itself proof of wrongdoing.

new_relations.boundary: The passage concerns ancient prophetic accusation and does not validate Tim's divine self-identification or every claim of insult.

new_relations.title: Face as presence, favor and opposition
new_relations.project_anchor: The project repeatedly uses face and eyes as recognition/accountability interfaces: look at me, hide your face, lie to my face, face God.
new_relations.source_direction: Project face/eyes vocabulary first; biblical face-function comparison later.

relation_argument.maximum_claim: Biblical face-language can function as a compact relational operator for presence, recognition, favor and opposition.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: It clarifies why 'face' carries more than appearance in the project's rhetoric.

new_relations.boundary: Biblical face idiom is metaphorical/theological and does not turn eye contact into a universal moral test.

new_relations.title: They will not listen
new_relations.project_anchor: A central Tim complaint is repeated speech without reception: he says he speaks and speaks while people refuse to listen.
new_relations.source_direction: Project repeated-not-listened-to motif first; Ezekiel comparison later.

biblical_sequence: Israel unwilling to listen because unwilling to listen to God
relation_argument.maximum_claim: Ezekiel is a strong literary neighbor for the 'speak repeatedly into refusal' structure.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: It strengthens the hearing motif while preserving the crucial boundary that resemblance to a prophetic situation does not establish prophetic office.

new_relations.boundary: The comparison does not prove Tim is Ezekiel, a prophet, or that disagreement equals rebellion against God.

new_relations.title: Humans must not become cargo
new_relations.project_anchor: Tim's trafficking language often means that a person is being treated as ownable, sellable, harvestable or consumable by a crowd/system.
new_relations.source_direction: Project trafficking/ownership critique first; biblical anti-sale/cargo cluster later.

biblical_sequence: Babylon's commerce culminates in human bodies/lives
relation_argument.maximum_claim: These texts provide a strong biblical anti-commodification cluster for the project's claim that persons should not be treated as tradable cargo.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: It is a much tighter biblical parallel than generic slavery imagery because the project repeatedly uses sale/ownership/trafficking language.

new_relations.boundary: Modern legal definitions of trafficking are specific and must be established by evidence; biblical comparison does not prove any particular modern trafficking allegation.

new_relations.title: Devouring people as extraction
new_relations.project_anchor: Tim sometimes describes abusive systems through flesh-eating, carcass, consumption and predation imagery.
new_relations.source_direction: Project consumption/predation imagery first; Micah comparison later.

biblical_sequence: skin/flesh/bones used as grotesque metaphor for exploitation
relation_argument.maximum_claim: Micah provides a vivid biblical precedent for describing exploitative rule through cannibalistic consumption imagery.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: It helps classify flesh-eating language as a moral metaphor of extraction rather than a literal biological claim.

new_relations.boundary: Micah's imagery is prophetic hyperbole; it does not justify violent or dehumanizing language toward modern opponents.

new_relations.title: From vomit to repentance to the Door
new_relations.project_anchor: The project independently clusters disgust/vomit, rebuke, repentance, Door and restored relation. Revelation 3 contains that sequence unusually densely.
new_relations.source_direction: Project disgust/vomit and Door/repentance vocabulary developed independently; Revelation 3 sequence identified later.

relation_argument.maximum_claim: Revelation 3 supplies one of the densest biblical sequences joining visceral rejection, correction, repentance, a Door, hearing and renewed communion.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: It ties together motifs that had been treated separately and shows that disgust imagery need not terminate in permanent exclusion.

new_relations.boundary: The Laodicean oracle addresses a church and is not a warrant for coercion, humiliation, or declaring oneself the speaker at the Door.

new_relations.title: Abomination is not the end of the route
new_relations.project_anchor: Tim's rhetoric often moves from 'abomination/disgusting' into 'repent,' 'apologize,' 'confess,' and then to the Son/Door.
new_relations.source_direction: Project abomination→repent→Door sequence first; Ezekiel/John structural comparison later.

biblical_sequence: God takes no pleasure in death
relation_argument.maximum_claim: The texts support a structural comparison in which condemnation is paired with a route of turning and renewed access rather than permanent essence.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: It prevents the abomination vocabulary from becoming a closed caste system and preserves repentance as a genuine change operator.

new_relations.boundary: John 10's gate saying concerns Jesus; it does not identify a modern person or project symbol as literally identical with Christ.

new_relations.title: What divine disgust is aimed at
new_relations.project_anchor: Tim's disgust language frequently targets arrogance, lying, plans to harm, false witness and perceived attacks on vulnerable people.
new_relations.source_direction: Project disgust vocabulary first; Proverbs content cluster later.

relation_argument.maximum_claim: Proverbs 6 shows that biblical divine aversion is often directed toward relational harms rather than mere aesthetic impurity.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: It helps explain 'disgust' as an ethical alarm category while avoiding the claim that Tim's targets are biblically adjudicated.

new_relations.boundary: The list is wisdom literature, not a tool for declaring disliked people abominations.
